title: Racing at altitude: when to arrive and how to pace
goal: Choose between arriving late and acclimatising first, and set a lower target power for a race at altitude.

steps.title: Day 1 is the low point, then it climbs
steps.text:
Eight elite cyclists were tested at sea level and again after 1, 7, 14 and 21 days at 2,340 m. On day 1, VO₂max was 12.8% below sea level and time to exhaustion 25.8% below [[c:rac-day1-claim]]. Then they came back:

| Step | VO₂max | Time to exhaustion |
|---|---|---|
| Day 1 to 7 | +3.2% | +6.0% |
| Day 7 to 14 | +4.8% | +5.7% |
| Day 14 to 21 | +0.7% (not significant) | +1.4% (not significant) |

Most of the gain came in the first two weeks, and little after [[c:rac-recover]]. The abstract does not say whether each % is a rise on the previous value or a share of sea level; here we treat it as a rise on the previous value. Either way, on day 14 VO₂max is still 5–6% below sea level (94.3% or 95.2%).

claims.text: On day 1 at 2,340 m, elite cyclists' VO₂max was 12.8% and time to exhaustion 25.8% below sea level.

evidence.quote: On Day 1, VO(2max) and time to exhaustion (at 80% of sea-level maximal power output) decreased by 12.8% (P<0.05) and 25.8% (P<0.05), respectively, compared with the corresponding sea-level values.

claims.text: Most of the recovery came by day 14 (VO₂max +3.2% by day 7, +4.8% more by day 14, +0.7% not significant by day 21).

evidence.quote: Subsequently, these parameters increased by 3.2% (P<0.05) and 6.0% (P<0.05) from Days 1 to 7, by 4.8% (P<0.05) and 5.7% (P<0.05) from Days 7 to 14, followed by 0.7% (P>0.05) and 1.4% (P>0.05) from Days 14 to 21, respectively.

steps.title: VO₂max on day 14
steps.problem: A cyclist has a sea-level VO₂max of 68 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. Using the 2,340 m data, what is VO₂max on day 14?
steps: Day 14: 61.2 × 1.048 = 64.1 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹, still about 6% below sea level.

steps.title: Arrive late, or acclimatise first
steps.text: The data suggest two clean plans. **Acclimatise:** the cyclists' study concluded that athletes racing at around 2,340 m should be there at least 14 days before [[c:rac-14d]]. **Arrive late:** accept the day-1 deficit and arrive as close to the start as you can. Mountain sickness hits 10–30% of people at 2,500–3,000 m, so rest on arrival. If you must train there, a review advises waiting about 2 days, then starting gradually [[c:rac-wait]]. A third route is [pre-acclimatisation](g:pre-acclimatisation) at home, in a tent; a review covers arrival timing and these strategies [[c:rac-review]].

claims.text: Endurance athletes competing around 2,340 m should expose themselves to that altitude at least 14 days before competition.

evidence.quote: These data suggest that endurance athletes competing at altitudes around 2340 m should expose themselves to this altitude at least 14 days before competition.

claims.text: After travelling to 2,500–3,000 m, one review advises waiting 2 days before gradually starting to train.

evidence.quote: It is possible to travel to altitudes of 2500-3000 m a.s.l., wait for 2 days, and then gradually start to train.

claims.text: A review gives data and advice on when to arrive at altitude and on sea-level pre-acclimatisation strategies.

evidence.quote: This brief review will offer data and current advice on when to arrive at altitude and various potential sea level-based pre-acclimatization strategies in an effort to maximize performance and minimize the risk of altitude sickness.

steps.title: Pacing: lower the target, race by effort
steps.text:
If aerobic power is down by the VO₂max loss, the sustainable target power falls by about the same share. A simple rule: **target power = sea-level power × (1 − 0.063 × km of altitude)**. It assumes the same share of VO₂max and the same efficiency, so it is a start, not a prediction.

The mistake is starting at sea-level pace: that pace now needs a bigger share of a smaller VO₂max, and a fixed hard speed becomes unsustainable much sooner (time to exhaustion fell 14.5% per 1,000 m in the chamber study). Heart rate also misleads: in acute exposure it is raised for a given effort [[c:rac-hr]]. Race by power or feel, with a lower first-half target.

claims.text: In acute exposure to altitude, heart rate and ventilation are raised.

evidence.quote: In acute exposure, ventilation and heart rate are elevated with a minimum reduction in stroke volume.

steps.title: A lower target power
steps.problem: A rider holds 300 W for a sea-level time trial. Using 6.3% per 1,000 m, what target do you set at 1,000 m?

steps.title: Thin air also pushes back less
steps.text:
Physics, not a study result: air drag is proportional to air density, and density falls with pressure. At 2,000 m the pressure is 596 ÷ 760 = 78% of sea level.

On a flat course, if drag were the only force, speed would follow (power ÷ density)^(1/3). With power down 12.6% (0.874) and density at 0.78: (0.874 ÷ 0.784)^(1/3) = 1.04, about 4% faster. Two things cut that: air higher up is usually colder and so denser (the standard atmosphere, 2 °C at 2,000 m, gives 82% and about +2%), and rolling resistance does not fall at all. So speed roughly holds.

On a climb gravity dominates, so the power loss shows in full. For runners, air drag is a smaller share of the cost, so there is less help.

points: On day 1 at 2,340 m, VO₂max was 12.8% below sea level; most of the recovery came in 2 weeks, little between weeks 2 and 3.
Pick a clear plan: arrive late and accept the deficit, or be there about 14 days before, with a 2-day wait before gentle training for mountain-sickness safety.
Target power at altitude about equals sea-level power × (1 − 0.063 × km); race by power or feel, not sea-level pace or heart rate.
Lower air density helps a rider on the flat but not on a climb.
The evidence is a few small studies at one altitude: treat the numbers as guides.

variants.stem: About how far below sea level was elite cyclists' VO₂max on their first day at 2,340 m?

options.why: Too small: that is the day 1 to 7 gain.
The loss per 1,000 m, not the day-1 total for 2,340 m.
Correct: 12.8% below sea level.
The fall in time to exhaustion, not in VO₂max.

variants.stem: A cyclist's sea-level VO₂max is 70 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. At 2,340 m it falls 12.8% on day 1, then rises 3.2% by day 7 and a further 4.8% by day 14 (each a rise on the previous value). What is VO₂max on day 14?

options.why: Assumed full recovery to the sea-level value.
Applied the two rises to the sea-level value and forgot the day-1 fall.
Stopped at the day-1 value.

variants.stem: A cyclist's sea-level VO₂max is 64 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. At 2,340 m it falls 12.8% on day 1, then rises 3.2% by day 7 and a further 4.8% by day 14 (each a rise on the previous value). What is VO₂max on day 14?

options.why: Assumed full recovery to the sea-level value.
Applied the two rises to the sea-level value and forgot the day-1 fall.
Stopped at the day-1 value.

variants.stem: A cyclist's sea-level VO₂max is 75 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. At 2,340 m it falls 12.8% on day 1, then rises 3.2% by day 7 (a rise on the day-1 value). What is VO₂max on day 7?

options.why: Assumed full recovery to the sea-level value.
Applied the rise to the sea-level value and forgot the day-1 fall.
Stopped at the day-1 value.

variants.stem: After travelling to 2,500–3,000 m, how long does one review advise waiting before gradually starting to train?

options.text: No wait: train as usual on day 1
options.why: Ignores mountain-sickness risk and the day-1 deficit.
Correct: wait about 2 days, then ease in.
Longer than the review says.
That is the time suggested for racing at 2,340 m, not the wait before gentle training.

variants.stem: Plan A: arrive at 2,340 m the day before the race. Plan B: arrive 3 weeks before. Which statement does the cyclists' study support?

options.text: Week 3 added little over week 2: the day 14 to 21 rise was not significant
options.why: Correct: +0.7% VO₂max and +1.4% time to exhaustion, neither significant.

options.text: Plan A is best because VO₂max is highest on the first day there
options.why: Day 1 was the lowest point: −12.8%.

options.text: Plan B restores the exact sea-level value, as the full curve shows
options.why: The study reports changes between days, not a full return to sea level.

variants.stem: The advice 'be there 14 days before' came from 8 elite cyclists at 2,340 m. Does it fit a race at 3,500 m?

options.text: Yes: acclimatisation always takes exactly 14 days at any altitude
options.why: Time courses differ with altitude and person; this is one small study.

options.text: Not necessarily: it is one small study at one altitude
options.why: Correct: eight athletes at one altitude cannot fix the plan for 3,500 m, where mountain sickness is also likelier.

options.text: No: before day 14 nothing changes at any altitude at all
options.why: Even in the study, gains appeared by day 7.

variants.stem: A rider holds 280 W in a sea-level time trial. Using 6.3% per 1,000 m, what target power do you set at 2,000 m on arrival?

options.why: Subtracted 12.6 as watts instead of a percentage.
Used the 14.5% per 1,000 m of time to exhaustion, not the VO₂max slope.
Kept the sea-level power: that ignores the loss.

variants.stem: A rider holds 320 W in a sea-level time trial. Using 6.3% per 1,000 m, what target power do you set at 1,500 m on arrival?

options.why: Subtracted 9.45 as watts instead of a percentage.
Used the 14.5% per 1,000 m of time to exhaustion, not the VO₂max slope.

variants.stem: A rider holds 250 W in a sea-level time trial. Using 6.3% per 1,000 m, what target power do you set at 2,500 m on arrival?

options.why: Subtracted 15.75 as watts instead of a percentage.
Used the 14.5% per 1,000 m of time to exhaustion, not the VO₂max slope.

variants.stem: A runner starts a 10 km race at 2,000 m at her sea-level pace and fades badly after 5 km. Why?

options.text: The same speed needs a larger share of a smaller VO₂max, so she reached her limit sooner
options.why: Correct: the pace was no longer sustainable at the lower aerobic power.

options.text: Dry mountain air dehydrated her within the first 5 km
options.why: Dry air adds fluid loss over hours and days; it does not explain a fade at sea-level pace in one 10 km race.

options.text: Her heart rate was lower than at sea level, so she ran too easily at first
options.why: Heart rate is raised in acute exposure, not lower.

variants.stem: A cyclist's power on arrival at 2,000 m is about 12.6% below sea level. On a flat time trial, which result fits the physics of air drag?

options.text: Speed falls by 12.6%, the same as power
options.why: Ignores that drag also falls with air density: speed follows the cube root of power over density.

options.text: Speed falls by much less than power, and may even hold
options.why: Correct: lower density cuts drag, which is most of the power cost on the flat.

options.text: Speed rises by 12.6%, because the air is thinner
options.why: Overstates it: power still fell and rolling resistance is unchanged.
